head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Negated copy of the numbers; Python's heap is a min-heap, so negatives make the largest number pop first
Turns the list into a heap in O(n)
Building a heap from existing data
The amount the total must be reduced by (true division keeps fractions)
Takes the current largest value and undoes the negation
Greedy: always halve the biggest number
Halving x removes x / 2 from the sum
Puts the halved value back (it may be halved again later)

p: Halving a number removes half of its current value from the sum, so the biggest number gives the biggest reduction in a single operation. Taking the biggest every time reaches the target in the fewest operations.

bullets: The answer is `3`.
Time: O(n + k log n) where k is the number of operations.
Space: O(n) for the heap.

2208.takeaway: Greedy with a max-heap (simulated by negating values): repeatedly halve the largest number until the total reduction reaches half of the original sum.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The number of windows of length k, i.e. the number of distinct operations
2 to the power e modulo 1,000,000,007 (fast modular exponentiation)

bullets: Flipping the same window twice cancels out, and the order of flips does not matter, so each of the `n - k + 1` windows is either used once or not at all.

Different choices give different strings: look at the leftmost chosen window. Its first position is flipped by that window only (later windows start further right and earlier windows are not chosen), so the first difference from the original appears exactly there.
So there are `2^(n - k + 1)` reachable strings. The actual bits of `s` do not matter.
For `1001` with k = 3 the four reachable strings are `1001`, `0111` (flip the first window), `1110` (flip the second) and `0000` (flip both).
Time: O(log n) for the modular power.
Space: O(1).

2450.takeaway: Each of the n - k + 1 window positions is an independent on/off switch, so the answer is 2 raised to that count, modulo 1,000,000,007.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: sum(w for _, w in items) < capacity
If all items together weigh less than the bag capacity, the bag can never be filled
sorted(items, key=lambda it: it[0] / it[1], reverse=True)
Items ordered by price per unit of weight, highest first
Weight we can take: the whole item, or only what still fits
Price of the part taken (price scales with weight)
Rounds to 5 decimals as the problem allows

p: `items = [[50,1],[10,8]]`, `capacity = 5`. Total weight 9 >= 5, so it is possible. Ratios: 50 and 1.25, so item `[50,1]` comes first.
bullets: Capacity reached 0, so the loop breaks and the answer is `55.0`.
For `items = [[100,30]]`, `capacity = 50` the total weight 30 is below 50, so the answer is `-1`.
Time: O(n log n) for sorting.
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

2548.takeaway: Fractional knapsack: take items in order of best price per weight, splitting the last one, and return -1 if the items cannot fill the bag.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Min-heap of the negative numbers seen so far (so the most negative pops first)
Remembering which negatives could be moved
Records each negative as a candidate to move to the end
The prefix sum has become negative, so a move is required
Removes the most negative number seen so far from the prefix (subtracting a negative adds back its size)
Counts that number as moved to the end

blocks.h: Why moving to the end works
p: Moving a number to the end deletes it from every earlier prefix. The total of the whole array is never negative, so after all moves the full prefix is fine. When a prefix becomes negative, moving the most negative number so far fixes it using the fewest moves, because it raises the prefix by the largest amount.

bullets: The answer is `1`: move `-5` to the end, giving `[3,-2,6,-5]` with prefix sums `3, 1, 7, 2`.
Time: O(n log n).
Space: O(n).

2599.takeaway: Scan left to right with a heap of negatives: whenever the prefix sum goes below zero, move the most negative number seen so far to the end (pop it from the prefix) and count one move.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The product 1 needs no digit factors; the smallest positive integer is 1
Keeps dividing out d while it divides n
Records the digit and shrinks n
A leftover prime factor larger than 7 cannot be a digit
Sorts ascending so the number is as small as possible
Smallest number from a multiset of digits
Converts the digits to text and joins them

p: Fewer digits means a smaller number, and dividing out large digits (9, then 8, ...) produces the fewest digits. Digit 1 would only lengthen the number, so it is never used. Sorting the digits ascending then gives the smallest arrangement.

bullets: For `n = 11` nothing divides it, `n` stays `11`, and the answer is `"-1"`.
Time: O(log n) divisions.
Space: O(log n) for the digits.

2847.takeaway: Divide n by digits 9 down to 2 to get the fewest digits, fail if anything is left over, then sort the digits ascending to form the smallest number.

p: `edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[2,3],[2,4]]`, `colors = [1,2,3,3,3]`. The visiting order is `0, 2, 4, 3, 1`, so the bottom-up order is `1, 3, 4, 2, 0`.

same[u]
best

rows: size[2] = 2; colours equal, same[2] stays True

bullets: The answer is `3`: the subtree rooted at node 2 (nodes 2, 3, 4).
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n).

3004.takeaway: Root the tree at 0, list nodes in DFS order, then walk that order backwards to accumulate subtree sizes and mark any subtree that contains a different colour.

Rightmost x covered by the current rectangle; nothing is covered at the start
This point is not covered, so start a new rectangle

Placing the rectangle as far right as possible

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Position (1-based) of the lower median among n(n+1)/2 subarray values
Median index for an even or odd count
Counts subarrays with at most k distinct values using a sliding window
Counts of values inside the window; deleting zero entries keeps len(cnt) equal to the distinct count
All subarrays ending at right whose start is in [left, right] are valid
Binary search range for the answer (distinct values per subarray)
At least `need` subarrays have <= mid distinct values, so the median is <= mid
Predicate that is monotone in mid

blocks.h: How the binary search finds the median
p: The median is the smallest `k` such that at least `need` subarrays have at most `k` distinct values. `at_most(k)` never decreases as `k` grows, so binary search applies.
`nums = [3,4,3,4,5]`: 15 subarrays, `need = (15 + 1) // 2 = 8`, `hi = 3` distinct values. Counting `at_most(2)` with the window:
bullets: `at_most(1) = 5` and `at_most(2) = 12`, `at_most(3) = 15`.
Binary search: `mid = 2` gives 12 >= 8, so `hi = 2`; `mid = 1` gives 5 < 8, so `lo = 2`. The answer is `2`.
Time: O(n log d), where d is the number of distinct values (each at_most is O(n)).
Space: O(d) for the counter.

3134.takeaway: Binary search the answer k: the median is the smallest k for which at least half of all subarrays have at most k distinct values, counted with a sliding window.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of X minus number of Y in the rectangle from (0,0) to (i,j) (2D prefix sum)
Equal X and Y means balance 0
Number of X in that rectangle
+1 for X, -1 for Y, 0 for '.' (booleans act as 0 or 1)
Turning a cell into a score
Inclusion-exclusion: add the top and left rectangles, subtract the overlap, add the new cell
The rectangle from the top-left corner to this cell qualifies

p: Every valid submatrix contains the top-left cell, so it is exactly the rectangle from `(0,0)` to some bottom-right cell `(i,j)`. There is one candidate per cell, and prefix sums read its balance in O(1).

bullets: The answer is `3`.
Time: O(m * n).
Space: O(m * n) for the two prefix tables.

3212.takeaway: A valid submatrix is a rectangle anchored at the top-left cell, so build 2D prefix sums of X-minus-Y and X counts and count the cells where the first is 0 and the second is positive.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Even values have no answer: a OR (a + 1) is always odd, because one of a and a + 1 is odd
Shifts x right by t and reads the lowest bit (shift binds tighter than &)
Counts the trailing 1 bits of x
Finding the run of low ones
A number with a single 1 at position t - 1
Clears the highest bit of that trailing run of ones
The smallest a whose OR with a + 1 gives x

p: If `a` ends in `0` followed by `t - 1` ones, then `a + 1` turns those ones into zeros and the zero into one. OR-ing them gives a run of `t` ones. So for `x` ending in `t` ones, `a = x` with bit `t - 1` (the top bit of the run) cleared. Clearing that bit gives the smallest such `a`.

bullets: The answer is `[9, 12, 15]`.
An even input such as 2 gives `-1`.
Time: O(n log max(nums)).
Space: O(n) for the result.

3315.takeaway: Count the trailing 1 bits t of x and clear bit t - 1: that gives the smallest a with a OR (a + 1) equal to x; even x has no answer.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: [c for c in str(n) if c != '0']
Keeps only the non-zero digit characters in order
Joins the digits into x; uses 0 when no digit remains (int of an empty string would fail)
Digit sum of x (zeros would not change it)

bullets: For `n = 1000` the digits are `1`, so `x = 1`, sum `1`, answer `1`.
For `n = 0` there are no digits, `x = 0`, answer `0`.
Time: O(d) where d is the number of digits.
Space: O(d).

3754.takeaway: Drop the zero digits, join the rest into x, and multiply x by its digit sum.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Maps a digit sum to the list of values with that digit sum
Fills the groups in ascending order, so each list is already sorted
cur: allowed values for the previous position; cnt[j]: number of valid arrays ending in cur[j]
Two-pointer over cur and a running total of cnt for entries <= v
Prefix sums over a sorted list
Adds every earlier value not larger than v
Arrays ending in v: sum of counts of all previous values <= v

p: `digitSum = [1,2]`. Values with digit sum 1: `1, 10, 100, 1000` (each count 1). Values with digit sum 2: `2, 11, 20, 101, 110, 200, 1001, 1010, 1100, 2000`.
bullets: For the site example `[25, 1]` the six values 799, 889, 898, 979, 988, 997 can precede 1000, so the answer is `6`.
If a digit sum has no value in range, or the first one has none, the function returns `0`.
Time: O(n * V) where V = 5001 values.
Space: O(V).

3883.takeaway: Group 0..5000 by digit sum, then for each position count arrays ending at v as the running sum of counts of all smaller-or-equal previous values using two pointers.
